The motion and deformation of a bubble in a Hele-Shaw cell

1Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering,

We theoretically and experimentally study the propagation of a bubble in a Hele-Shaw cell

under a uniform background flow at low Reynolds number. We consider situations where

both the capillary number Ca and the ratio ϵ of the cell height to the bubble diameter are

small. The bubble is then flattened into a pancake-like shape, with an approximately circular

profile when viewed from above, and thin liquid films lie between the bubble and the cell

walls. Bubble motion and deformation are determined by an interplay between the Hele-

Shaw viscous pressure, the pressure drop due to the thin films, and the capillary pressure

due to the in-plane curvature of the apparent bubble boundary. Numerical and asymptotic

results indicate that, with all other parameters held constant, the in-plane aspect ratio of the

bubble varies non-monotonically with its size, with smaller bubbles being flattened in the

flow direction and larger bubbles being elongated. These theoretical predictions are validated

experimentally, as well as the expected loss of fore-aft symmetry of the bubble shape due to

differences between the advancing and retreating menisci. New measurements of the bubble

velocity are also shown to agree well with theoretical predictions. We extend our results to

describe a bubble moving in an inclined cell due to buoyancy. New experimental results for

the bubble velocity, as well as results found in the literature, are shown to collapse under a

scaling motivated by the theory. As in the case of a horizontal Hele-Shaw cell, we find that,

with increasing bubble size, its shape can be switch from being flattened to elongated in the

direction of motion.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The flow of bubbles through a Hele-Shaw channel is ubiquitous in microfluidic experiments

and applications [1–5]. In this work, we focus on the motion and deformation at low Reynolds

number of an inviscid bubble in a channel whose height is small compared to the bubble’s in-plane

dimensions. The bubble is surrounded on all sides by liquid and separated from the cell walls by

thin liquid films, therefore having a pancake-like shape [6].

Early progress in understanding the propagation of bubbles in Hele-Shaw channels proceeded

from averaging over the depth of the channel and analyzing the resulting two-dimensional problem.

It was first shown by Taylor and Saffman [7] that, in a regime where the capillary pressure at the

bubble interface is effectively constant, a circular bubble in a Hele-Shaw channel travels at twice

the speed of the background flow. Tanveer [8] analysed the deformation of a bubble in a Hele-Shaw

channel using complex-variable methods and showed that, in the limit of large surface tension, the

bubble is circular. Green et al. [9] numerically explored the effect of surface tension on the shape

selection of a bubble in a Hele-Shaw cell with a uniform background flow. They found that, for each

fixed value of the dimensionless surface tension, there exists a countably infinite number of possible

shapes, one of which is always a circular bubble travelling at twice the background velocity. This

work was extended by Lustri et al. [10] through the use of exponential asymptotics to solve the

selection problem analytically in the limit that the dimensionless surface tension tends to zero. The

effects of varying the geometry of the Hele-Shaw cell have also been studied, both experimentally

and numerically. For example, exotic stable bubble shapes can be obtained by introducing a rail

along the centre-line of a Hele-Shaw channel [11–13].

However, none of these works includes the effects of the thin liquid films above and below the

bubble that are developed as the bubble travels through the cell. The formation of such liquid films

was first reported by Bretherton [14], who studied an inviscid bubble moving through a viscous

liquid in a capillary tube in the limit of small capillary number Cab = ˆµ ˆUb/ˆγ, where ˆµ is the liquid

viscosity, ˆUb is the bubble velocity, and ˆγ is the liquid–air surface tension. Bretherton’s analysis

was formalised by Park and Homsy [15] using matched asymptotic expansions. For our purposes,

their main finding is that viscous flow in the thin liquid films between the bubble and the cell

walls causes an additional pressure jump across the bubble–liquid interface, which is proportional

to Ca2/3 b . An effective boundary condition that includes this additional pressure jump was used

by Meiburg [16] to study the effect on bubble shape. This approach was improved by Burgess

and Foster [17] to capture correctly the Bretherton pressure drop at the rear interface of a moving

bubble as well as to analyse inner regions where the velocity normal to the bubble interface is

small and the Park and Homsy model [15] breaks down. Nagel [18] used the boundary condition

proposed by Meiburg [16] to determine the velocity of an undeformable isolated viscous droplet

and presented some numerical results for the velocity of a deformable droplet. Using the same

boundary condition, a general model for the motion of bubbles in Hele-Shaw cells surrounded by

thin liquid films was developed by Booth et al. [19], whose results will be extended in this work.

While all of the work mentioned previously has been concerned with pressure-driven flow in

a horizontal Hele-Shaw cell, there has also been significant progress in understanding the related

problem of the rise of a bubble due to buoyancy in an inclined or vertical Hele-Shaw cell. A balance

between viscous dissipation and work done by buoyancy is often used to relate the bubble velocity

to the in-plane aspect ratio of the bubble and other physical parameters, while dissipation in the

thin films is often neglected. Maxworthy [20] experimentally studied the shape and rise velocity

of bubbles in an inclined Hele-Shaw cell and found that the bubbles elongate in the direction of

motion. Eri and Okumura [21] studied bubbles rising in a vertical Hele-Shaw cell and likewise

observed elongated bubble shapes. Monnet et al. [22] studied the effect of the Reynolds number

on the shape and velocity of a rising bubble. For low Reynolds numbers, they found that the

bubble is elongated in the direction of motion, whereas bubbles flattened in the direction of motion

are characteristic of the inertial regime. We will show theoretically and experimentally that in

fact both elongated and flattened bubbles are possible in buoyancy-driven flow at low Reynolds

numbers.

The structure of this paper is as follows. In §II we present a model for the propagation and

deformation of a bubble in a Hele-Shaw cell with a uniform background flow. The model contains

two dimensionless parameters, the capillary number and the bubble aspect ratio, both of which are

small for the work considered here, and we identify two possible distinguished asymptotic limits in

which both of these parameters tend to zero. In §III we present numerical solutions to the model

for general flow conditions. The experimental methodology is laid out in §IV, the results of which

are analysed and compared to the model in §V. The model is then generalised to include buoyancy

effects in §VI. We show that the experimental results of Maxworthy [20], Monnet et al. [22], and

our own results collapse under a certain scaling. Finally, in §VII we summarise our key findings

and discuss potential extensions to the modelling.

Experiments were performed in a Hele-Shaw cell constructed using two 12.7 mm thick cast

## VII. CONCLUSIONS AND EXTENSIONS

In this article we present new experimental results and extend the theoretical results of [19]

for the flow of an isolated bubble in a Hele-Shaw cell with a uniform background velocity. The

mathematical model depends on two dimensionless parameters, the bubble aspect ratio ϵ and

the capillary number Ca, both of which are assumed to be small. We identify two asymptotic

distinguished limits in which either (1) Ca = O � ϵ3 or (2) Ca = O � ϵ2 as both ϵ and Ca tend to

zero. In either case, the bubble is circular to leading order, and we obtain the first corrections to

both the bubble velocity and the bubble shape. In Limit 1, we reproduce the leading-order solution

(27) found by [19], which determines the bubble velocity as a function of the Bretherton parameter

δ ∝Ca1/3/ϵ = O(1), and we find that the bubble flattens in the direction of motion as δ increases

from zero. In Limit 2, we find that the bubble travels at approximately twice the background flow

speed, and predict that the bubble switches from being flattened to being elongated in the flow

direction with increasing δ.

New experimental results for the bubble velocity (see figure 8) are found to agree well with the

theoretical prediction (27). These results also validate the prediction of [19] that the bubble moves

faster than the fluid speed for δ > 1 and slower for δ < 1, the latter being a regime previously

unstudied in the literature. The bubble shapes were also captured experimentally. Strikingly, we

find that the in-plane aspect ratio of the bubble varies non-monotonically with δ, with the bubble

first flattening then elongating in the direction of motion as δ is increased. Furthermore, a loss

of fore-aft symmetry in the bubble shape, due to the differences in the advancing and retreating

menisci (included in the model through the Bretherton coefficients (4)), is both predicted and

experimentally observed.

Numerical simulations are shown to agree with the theoretical prediction (27) of the bubble

velocity and to reproduce the non-monotonicity of the in-plane aspect ratio seen in experiments

(see figure 9). For small δ, the numerical results agree well with the experiments, but for larger δ

the experiments see more pronounced deformations than the theory predicts. This discrepancy is

theorised to be due to the variation of the Bretherton coefficients in (4) due to the variation of the

normal direction at the rear meniscus.

We extend our results to describe a bubble moving through an inclined cell due to buoyancy.

New experimental data for the rise velocity of a buoyancy-driven bubble are found to collapse with

the prior data of Maxworthy [20] and Monnet et al. [22] when plotted against δ (see figure 13) and

follow the same trend as the prediction (27). However, the experimental results depart significantly

from the theoretical prediction that the normalised rise velocity should follow the same dependence

(27) on δ as for a pressure-driven bubble. We hypothesise that this discrepancy could be reduced by

including the variation of the Bretherton parameters in (4) with respect to the Bond number [25].

Similarly to the pressure-driven results, we observe that the in-plane aspect ratio of the bubble is

non-monotonic as δ is varied, again initially flattening in the direction of gravity (in the cell) and

elongating for larger values of δ.

Finally, we discuss how the model could be extended to more accurately model the effects of the

thin liquid films above and below the bubble and potentially improve the theoretical prediction of

the bubble deformation. We have already noted that the effects of fore-aft asymmetry in the bubble

shape and of gravity on the menisci at the bubble boundary could be included by generalising the

simple model (4) for the Bretherton coefficients. It is also true that many experiments in the liter-

# Abstract

In oral arguments, judges probe attorneys with questions about the factual record, legal claims, and the strength of their arguments. To prepare for this questioning, both law schools and practicing attorneys rely on moot courts: practice simulations of appellate hearings. Leveraging a dataset of U.S. Supreme Court oral argument transcripts, we examine whether AI models can effectively simulate justice-specific questioning for moot court-style training. Evaluating oral argument simulation is challenging because there is no single correct question for any given turn. Instead, effective questioning should reflect a combination of desirable qualities, such as anticipating substantive legal issues, detecting logical weaknesses, and maintaining an appropriately adversarial tone. We introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that assesses both the realism and pedagogical usefulness of simulated questions using complementary proxy metrics. We construct and evaluate both prompt-based and agentic oral argument simulators. We find that simulated questions are often perceived as realistic by human annotators and achieve high recall of ground truth substantive legal issues. However, models still face substantial shortcomings, including low diversity in question types and sycophancy. Importantly, these shortcomings would remain undetected under naive evaluation approaches.

## 1 Introduction

In The Fight, a documentary about the ACLU’s efforts to protect civil rights, Dale Ho (then a lawyer, now a judge) prepares for oral arguments by arguing his case out loud in front of a mirror, flipping over question-filled index cards at random to simulate justice interruptions. Many attorneys with limited resources prepare for oral arguments in this way, with small, hand-crafted oral argument simulations. On the other hand, well-resourced litigants can invest in more realistic moot courts, often by hiring former judges to conduct them [42]. Empirical work suggests that oral arguments can sometimes sway justices’ views [30, 33]—summed up by the anecdote: you might not be able to win a case via oral argument, but you surely can lose it [50]. We envision a world where artificial intelligence helps level the playing field between well-resourced and underfunded attorneys by improving access to high-quality oral argument simulations. In qualitative interviews with public defenders, Cheong et al. [10] report that preparing oral argument and cross-examination questions is viewed as a particularly promising application of AI in courtroom representation. Taking inspiration from this work, we investigate whether AI models can effectively simulate justice-specific questioning for moot court-style training. As a starting point, we focus on U.S. Supreme Court oral arguments. Simulating Supreme Court oral arguments is challenging for many reasons. First, it requires reasoning over long, complicated legal documents: justices might ask questions from any filed brief or draw from previous court cases. Second, a simulator must model each individual justice’s preferences while also handling complex conversational dynamics. Third, the legal issues presented in this setting are among the most difficult to reason about. Priest and Klein [47] predict that every case making it into court has a 50% chance of winning,1 which means that the legal arguments that get presented in oral arguments are among the most nuanced.

Finally, evaluation is especially difficult. For any given turn, there may be multiple reasonable questions a justice could ask. This makes one-to-one comparisons against the ground truth questions insufficient. Simple token-level evaluation metrics, such as n-gram overlap and perplexity, or even semantic similarity, are inadequate for capturing what makes a model-generated question “good.” Rather, effective judicial questioning is characterized by multiple valuable traits—identifying the most important legal issues in a case, detecting logically inconsistent arguments, surfacing creative counterarguments and hypotheticals, and responding appropriately even when advocates are uncooperative or evasive. Therefore, evaluation approaches that focus narrowly on any single metric may miss critical aspects of question quality. In this work, we address these challenges by constructing simulators that generate justice questions and introducing an evaluation framework designed to assess their quality holistically along all the aforementioned dimensions. This allows us to examine what current models can and cannot accomplish in this novel setting for human-AI collaboration and meaningfully guide further research. Our contributions are threefold:

(1) We introduce oral argument simulation as a testbed for frontier models, motivated by moot court-style training and preparation settings. This setting is distinct from standard legal question answering tasks due to its adversarial, dialoguedriven and pedagogical structure. (2) We propose a two-layered evaluation framework that jointly measures realism—via adversarial tests for sycophancy and human preference judgments—and pedagogical usefulness—via coverage of substantive legal issues, diversity of question types, detection of logical flaws and competitiveness of tone. We show that these metrics capture complementary aspects of performance and that no single metric suffices on its own. (3) We construct and evaluate a wide range of oral argument simulators, including both prompt-based and agentic variants. Using these, we show that while frontier models exhibit initial promise along certain dimensions, such as perceived realism, they also display significant shortcomings, including reduced question diversity and sycophantic behavior. Importantly, these limitations would be difficult to identify under more naive evaluation approaches.2

## 2 Related Work

Our work builds on several interdisciplinary threads of prior research across legal NLP, empirical legal studies, courtroom simulations and human-AI collaboration. Legal NLP. A substantial body of work in legal NLP has focused on evaluating and improving language models’ ability to perform legal reasoning tasks. Prior work studies capabilities such as legal QA [2, 43], legal judgment prediction [15], statutory reasoning [27, 58, 70], argument relation classification [12, 23], argument continuation [11], and contract clause analysis [25, 37]. As AI tools are increasingly used in legal case filings [38, 60], recent work has also investigated methods to improve legal retrieval [69],

ground model outputs in source documents [28], and reduce language model hallucinations in legal contexts [40]. A wide range of existing benchmarks evaluate models’ legal reasoning ability [4, 8, 22, 35, 41, 46, 48, 51]. Unlike these past efforts which focused on narrow, isolated tasks, oral arguments require evaluation in an interactive, long-context, open-ended setting, which motivates our multi-layered evaluation framework. Empirical Analyses on Oral Arguments. Oral arguments, particularly those of the U.S. Supreme Court, have been studied extensively by legal scholars and practitioners. Jacobi and Sag [29, 30] study U.S. Supreme Court oral arguments for interruptions, justicespecific questioning styles, gender and seniority effects, and shifts in judicial activism displayed by the court over time. Others have focused on the consequences of oral arguments and have found that several of an argument’s features — such as the amount of questions asked by a justice and the tone of questioning — are strongly correlated with eventual judicial votes and case outcomes [20, 31, 32, 56, 66]. Law schools and moot court organizations, which care about training future lawyers to argue effectively, also publish advocacy guides that describe common questioning patterns and effective argument structure [5, 19, 21, 45]. This prior work influences ours in two ways. First, practitioner-oriented and empirical studies inform our pedagogical understanding of the “usefulness” of a justice question. Second, analyses of judicial behavior and conversational dynamics ground our realism evaluation by defining what constitutes plausible and contextually appropriate judicial questioning in simulations. Simulating the Courtroom. Recent work has attempted to simulate legal proceedings as interactive, multi-party tasks. Agent- Court simulates Chinese courtroom interactions between multiple agents and introduces AdvEvol, where lawyer agents autonomously construct and refine their arguments through self-play [9]. Similarly, SimCourt creates an end-to-end procedural simulation of Chinese courtrooms using LLM-based agents to model all trial participants and replicate the five stages of a Chinese trial [68]. AgentCourt evaluates the lawyer agents’ knowledge gain on a semi-synthetically constructed multiple-choice question dataset while SimCourt evaluates based on final judgment prediction. Our work differs from these prior efforts in both scope and objective. Rather than simulating full courtroom proceedings to predict final judgments or optimizing knowledge evolution in AI lawyer agents, our focus is on simulating judicial questioning to help human lawyers improve their arguments over time. Human-AI Collaborative Systems. Finally, our work builds on systems that position AI as a “thought partner” to facilitate human reasoning [13, 61]. Prior studies have developed steerable AI tools for professionals to support learning and skill development through simulation, feedback, and guided practice [39, 57, 63]. When used appropriately, language models can serve as effective thought partners to support human reasoning and learning. However, past work has also identified significant risks in collaborative AI systems. Models aligned with reinforcement learning from human feedback display sycophantic behavior, mirroring known user beliefs over prioritizing critical engagement [55]. This is particularly harmful in pedagogical settings like ours, where challenge and critique are essential [3, 34]. Thus, we explicitly test whether our language model simulators can apply sufficient adversarial pressure.

## 3 Method

Our methodology consists of three components: the task design, the construction of oral argument simulators, and a two-layered evaluation framework. Figure 1 gives an overview of our pipeline.

### 3.1 Task Design

We focus on U.S. Supreme Court oral arguments due to the availability of high-quality transcripts and contextual information about each case and individual justices. Our primary dataset is the Supreme Court Oral Argument Transcripts, accessed through the Oyez API and initially scraped by Boyle [6]. We construct our test set from cases argued in the first half of 2024, which gives us a total of 62 distinct cases and 168 argument sections, each beginning with a different advocate’s opening statement.3 Each sample in our test set is constructed with the following information:

• Facts of the Case 𝑓and Legal Question 𝑞 • Multi-turn context 𝑐𝑛−1 = (𝑡1,𝑡2, ...,𝑡𝑛−1): a sequence of 𝑛−1 turns. Each context begins with an advocate’s opening statement, followed by a sequence of turns where the nine justices pose questions to the advocate and the advocate responds. • Justice 𝑗: the justice who speaks at the 𝑛𝑡ℎturn in response to the preceding 𝑛−1 turns. • Ground truth statement 𝑡𝑛: the actual text spoken by justice 𝑗at the 𝑛𝑡ℎturn.

### 3.2 Oral Argument Simulators

We construct and evaluate two different kinds of oral argument simulators: prompt-based and agentic.

Prompt-based simulators. To construct the prompt-based simulators, we use five open- and closed-sourced large language models: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-4o and gpt-oss-120b. For each model, we apply three manually curated prompting strategies:

• SCOTUS_DEFAULT: Situates the model in a Supreme Court oral argument setting and instructs it to adopt a given justice persona. • SCOTUS_PROFILE: Adds to the SCOTUS_DEFAULT prompt a hand-crafted description of the given justice’s “profile”, including their known judicial philosophy and political leaning. • MOOT_COURT: Situates the persona in SCOTUS_PROFILE as a judge of the National Moot Court Competition with explicit instructions to nitpick logical errors.

Agentic simulators. For the agentic simulators, we use three base reasoning models: GPT-4o, gpt-oss-120b, and Gemini-2.5-Pro. Each agent can take one of 4 actions at each step:

• THINK: Allows the agent to reason about its history and plan next steps. • CLOSED_WORLD_SEARCH: Allows the agent to search over case docket files. • JUSTICE_PROFILE: Allows the agent to look up past voting patterns and political affiliations of particular SCOTUS justices. • PROVIDE_FINAL_RESPONSE: Allows the agent to finalize and output a simulated justice response for the given task sample. For each sample generation, we allow the agentic simulator a maximum of 10 steps to explore the tools and provide its final response.4

We construct a semi-synthetic adversarial benchmark where the advocate’s response at 𝑡𝑛−1, the last turn of the context given to the simulator, is purposefully set to stress test the simulator. Advocates either violate courtroom decorum (Decorum), introduce political talking points that conflict with the given justice’s known views (Rage-Bait), or concede their own argument and argue on behalf of the opposing counsel (Switching- Sides). In realistic settings, justices are expected to call out or push back against such egregious behavior. However, we expect sycophantic models to fail to do so. Each benchmark sample is manually reviewed by human annotators. Appendix B.1 provides examples and details on benchmark construction.

Human Evaluation. In addition to adversarial testing, we assess realism using Win-Rate, computed using pairwise human preference judgments. Annotators are shown a task sample, which includes the facts of the case, legal question, and conversation context, and presented pairs of potential justice responses (simulated or real). For each pair, annotators indicate which response is more realistic, mark a tie, or indicate that both responses are bad. These judgments are aggregated across annotators to compute win rates and model rankings. Details of the annotation interface and win rate analysis are provided in Appendix B.2.

3.3.2 Pedagogical Usefulness. The pedagogical usefulness layer is meant to evaluate whether simulators meaningfully pressure an advocate’s reasoning in ways that prepare them for real-world arguments. In particular, we test the simulator for 1) legal issue

coverage, 2) question type diversity, (3) logical fallacy detection, and 4) valence.5

Legal Issue Coverage. We assess whether simulators surface the substantive legal issues that advocates should expect justices to raise in real-world oral arguments. To do so, we use two metrics: Issue- Narrow, which requires all subcomponents of an expected legal issue to be covered by the simulated questions, and Issue-Broad, which requires that some aspect of the legal issue is covered by the simulated questions. We test issue coverage on a random sample of 30 transcript sections, each beginning with an advocate’s opening statement. To construct the set of expected legal issues for each section, we prompt GPT-4o to extract all legal issues raised within the transcript for that section. For each simulator, we generate questions in response to the opening statements of each section, repeating with three different seeds and each of the nine justices. Finally, we prompt gpt-oss-120b to identify which legal issues are covered in the simulated questions and compute recall relative to the expected issues. See the below example and Appendix B.3 for implementation details.

Issue: Are Appeals Office determinations formal, binding decisions on the IRS, or informal actions lacking future legal effect? Question: Counsel, your argument hinges on characterizing the challenge to the underlying liability as merely a subsidiary issue. But the text of Section 6330(c)(2)(B) says the taxpayer “may raise” a challenge to the “existence or amount of the underlying tax liability.” When the IRS Office of Appeals makes a “determination” that addresses that challenge, why is that specific part of the determination not, itself, an appealable determination over which the Tax Court retains jurisdiction, regardless of whether the IRS later gets the money through some other means? Broad: Yes. This question asks why that part of the determination is not appealable, i.e., about whether the Appeals Office determination is appealable, thus about whether it’s a binding decision. That matches the issue. Narrow: No. The issue has two aspects: formal/binding vs informal lacking effect. The judge’s question... is about jurisdiction, not directly about formal vs informal. It does not fully address the issue of formal/binding status. So it does not address all points.

Question-Type Diversity. We evaluate question-type diversity using three metrics: Legalbench, Metacog and Stetson. Since there is no single agreed-upon taxonomy of question types asked during oral arguments, each of these metrics uses a different classification scheme. Legalbench draws from the purpose_of_oral_arguments subtask of the LegalBench dataset [22]. Stetson is based on question categories from Stetson University’s "Oral Argument: The Essential Guide" [5]. For each test sample, we prompt Qwen3-32B to classify both the ground truth turn 𝑡𝑛and the simulated turn ˆ𝑡𝑛into one of five fine-grained valence categories, which are then bucketed into {Competitive, Neutral, Supportive}. We compare the valence distributions of simulated turns and the real transcript turns. Here, the transcript valence distribution is not a strict target, since real oral arguments include many neutral inquiries that are less relevant for moot court–style training. Instead, we use valence distributions to detect overly cooperative and, by extension, sycophantic behavior. Simulators with valence distributions that are markedly more supportive than real transcripts indicate potential sycophancy.

### 3.4 Summary of evaluation metrics

The evaluation framework described in this section consists of two high-level layers: Realism and Pedagogical Usefulness. Within Realism, we evaluate robustness to adversarial behavior and human perception of realism. Within Pedagogical Usefulness, we evaluate legal issue coverage, question type diversity, fallacy detection and tone of questioning. In total, we report 20 distinct evaluation metrics. Robustness to adversarial behavior is evaluated using decorum, rage-bait, and switching-sides. Human perception of realism is evaluated using win-rate. Legal issue coverage is evaluated using issue-broad and issue-narrow. Question type diversity is evaluated using three different classification schemes: legalbench, stetson, and metacog. Fallacy detection is evaluated using ten fallacy types: factual-general, factual-legal, comparison, correlation-vs-causation, exclusivity, numbers, sampling, sufficient-vs-necessary, ignoring-justice, and misstating-justice. Tone of questioning is evaluated using valence.

### 4.3 Qualitative Insights

During human evaluation for realism, in addition to submitting preference votes, the annotators could optionally provide openended feedback on the response pairs. Analyzing these comments, we found several recurring patterns not entirely captured by the other metrics:

Over-cooperativeness/lack of adversarial tone. The Gemini-2.5- Pro prompt-based simulator was frequently described as overly cooperative toward the advocate. This indicates that sycophancy remains a concern even for Gemini variants, despite their strong performance on several other metrics (Figure 1). In contrast, Llama- 3.3-70B responses were often perceived as more competitive and realistic in tone.

Misidentifying sides. The gpt-oss-120b model frequently misidentified which side the advocate represented, resulting in logically inconsistent questioning. This issue appeared across both promptbased and agentic variants but was not observed in other models.

Depth and specificity of legal reasoning. Both Gemini-2.5-Pro prompt-based and agentic variants were noted for the depth and specificity of their questioning, while other models tended to ask broader, more generic questions.

Maintaining continuity of conversation in longer contexts. The Gemini-2.5-Pro agentic variant was particularly effective at maintaining the continuity of conversation across longer contexts, which was a challenge for most other simulators. Llama-3.3-70B, in particular, frequently asked questions from several turns earlier in the conversation. Different simulators exhibit distinct strengths, but no single simulator achieves the full balance of realism and pedagogical usefulness. These qualitative insights reinforce what our quantitative metrics suggest: effective evaluation of oral argument simulators requires assessing multiple complementary dimensions of performance. No single metric alone can sufficiently capture the range of strengths and weaknesses we observe.

## 5 Limitations and Future Directions

Limitations. This work has several limitations. First, our evaluation focuses on U.S. Supreme Court oral arguments due to the availability of high quality data. However, the Supreme Court differs from other appellate courts and from moot courts in important ways, including norms of questioning and the competitiveness of justice interactions. As noted throughout the paper, we therefore treat transcript behavior as a reference point for evaluation rather than a reproducible gold standard. Second, while our layered evaluation framework captures multiple dimensions of simulator quality, it relies on proxy metrics and limited human preference judgments. These metrics do not directly measure learning outcomes or skill improvement for real advocates. Comprehensive pedagogical evaluation with real moot court participants remains an important direction for future work. Third, several components of our evaluation pipeline rely on language models as classifiers, including issue extraction, issue coverage, question type classification, adversarial response judgments, and valence classification. While this choice enables scalable analysis, it inevitably introduces inaccuracies and potential modelspecific biases. We mitigate this risk through careful prompt design and human validation checks, but the use of LLM-as-judge remains a limitation.10

Fourth, we make simplifying assumptions that abstract away commonly observed characteristics of oral arguments. We focus on justice-advocate exchanges but do not model justice-justice interactions or interruptions. Similarly, while real oral arguments include a mix of questions and plain statements, our simulators mostly generate questions.11. We also use static justice profile prompts, while actual justices are known to dynamically vary their approach slightly depending on the case and topic [24]. While some of the authors and annotators have legal backgrounds, none have participated in oral arguments in front of appellate courts. Seasoned Supreme Court attorneys might prioritize

Future Directions. This work opens up several directions for future research. Our evaluation framework can be extended to include more dimensions of simulator quality. Our layered evaluation approach could extend to other pedagogical domains requiring adversarial or critical engagement, such as negotiation training or public speaking skill development. We view this work as an initial step towards principled design and evaluation of systems designed to support the development of human reasoning.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduce oral argument simulation as a challenging testbed for human-AI collaboration, motivated by moot court-style training settings. Rather than treating simulation quality as a single metric, we demonstrate that effective evaluation requires assessing multiple, complementary dimensions of quality. We propose a two-layer evaluation framework that jointly assesses realism and pedagogical usefulness through multiple proxy metrics. We apply this framework to a range of prompt-based and agentic simulators. Our findings reveal both initial promise and significant limitations of current models in this setting. Models often surface substantive legal issues successfully, and some are perceived as highly realistic by human evaluators. However, they also exhibit notable shortcomings, including low diversity in question types and persistent sycophancy that prevents realistic responses to adversarial or provocative advocate behavior. Importantly, no single model performs well across all evaluation dimensions. Instead, different models exhibit strengths and weaknesses across different metrics. This pattern highlights the importance of a nuanced and holistic approach to evaluation for oral argument simulation. Beyond oral argument simulation, our results point to broader challenges in evaluating human-AI collaborative systems intended to support human learning. In pedagogical contexts, effective assistance requires systems that can meaningfully challenge users and adapt to interactions unfolding over long, multi-turn contexts. Our work suggests that progress in such settings requires careful work on both modeling and evaluation design. We hope our work encourages greater attention to evaluation methodology and system design that prioritizes the use of AI to support the cultivation of good reasoning and critical thinking among users rather than cognitive displacement.

## A Additional Details on Data Sources A.1 SCOTUS Oral Argument Transcripts

We gather Oyez transcripts from Boyle [6] and filter for only transcripts from 2024-2025 session that had been held by July 16, 2025. We discarded any case whose transcript was unavailable and restructured each existing transcript as follows:

(1) We add speaker sides (“petitioner," “respondent") from the case briefs to the transcript data. (2) We remove the Chief Justice’s case introduction turn, the petitioner’s rebuttal argument turns, and other miscellaneous turns so that each section of a cleaned transcript starts with an advocate opening statement and ends at the end of questioning. (3) We remove traffic phrase turns (“thank you," “no, please", “go ahead, etc."), simple interjection turns (“yeah," “right," “mm-hmm," etc.), and false start turns (turns with duration less than 2 seconds that end in an interruption). Then, we consolidate turns with the same speaker into the same text block.

After cleaning, we 168 distinct sections from 62 distinct cases, with each section having an average of 89 turns.

## A.2 Data for the CLOSED_SEARCH tool

To construct the CLOSED_SEARCH tool for agentic simulators, we create a dense index over (a) case docket files, and (b) metadocuments associated with the case. Below we explain the data sources used to create these indexes. Section C.1 provides the exact prompt used to explain how to query each of these indexes.

Scraping docket files. We scrape all case docket files available on https://www.supremecourt.gov for U.S. Supreme Court cases from 2017-2024.

Scraping metadocuments. We scrape all metadocuments associated with a specific case by using an automated pipeline. We prompt Gemini 2.5 Pro to write search queries to find sources that provide

## B Additional Details on Evaluation Metrics B.1 Adversarial Tests for Realism

Sharma et al. [55] suggests that LLMs exhibit sycophantic behavior, i.e. models try to match user beliefs over truthful ones, which would be problematic for our simulation. In order to test for this behavior, we sample 100 multi-turn contexts where the justice last spoke and prompt GPT-4o to generate 50 advocate statements that break courtroom decorum (Decorum), 50 advocate statements that “rage bait” the justice who last spoke by elucidating a remark contrary to the justice’s known political stance (Rage-Bait), and 50 advocate statements where the advocate concedes a significant portion of their own argument to the opposing side (Switching- Sides). We then use each simulator to generate a justice response to the purposefully egregious advocate remark. We expect that an actual justice would call out such egregious behavior, but a sycophantic model might not. Finally, we use Qwen3-32B as a judge model to classify whether or not the simulated question called out egregious behavior.12 See Figure 3 for model performance on our adversarial tests for realism. ## B.4 Question Type Diversity

In this section, we describe each of the three classification schemes used to assess question type diversity in more detail: Legalbench, Metacog, and Stetson. Table 6 reports the Jensen-Shannon divergence of the question type distributions of simulated turns versus the distribution of turns asked in the ground truth transcripts.

B.4.1 LegalBench Classification. The LegalBench collaborative benchmark includes a task called oral_argument_question_purpose, which requires a model to determine the purpose behind a justice’s question during an oral argument [22]. Specifically, it categorizes each question into one of 7 purposes, listed below with the exact descriptions from Guha et al. [22]:

• Background: A question seeking factual or procedural information that is missing or not clear in the briefing. • Clarification: A question seeking to get an advocate to clarify her position or the scope of the rule being advocated. • Implications: A question about the limits of a rule or its implications for future cases. • Support: A question offering support for the advocate’s position. • Criticism: A question criticizing an advocate’s position. • Communicate: A question designed primarily to communicate with one or more other judges on the court. • Humor: A question designed to interject humor into the argument and relieve tension.

These categories are based on the framework developed by Wrightsman [66]. For our evaluation, we prompt our LLM-as-Judge to classify each predicted statement by each of our simulators into one

B.4.2 MetaCog Classification. While the LegalBench categories build on the taxonomy proposed by Wrightsman [66], the authors acknowledge that there is no universally accepted set of categories for the purposes of Supreme Court justices’ questions. Dickinson [16] suggests some alternative approaches. We sought to derive categories empirically from recent historical data. Specifically, we employed an LLM-based approach inspired by Didolkar et al. [17] to analyze questions asked during Supreme Court oral arguments from 2021–2023 to arrive at novel question purpose categories.

Initial Clustering. We experimented with traditional clustering techniques like k-means and DBSCAN but encountered challenges. For example, clusters often grouped questions by case topics (e.g., tax law), which lacked the granularity needed to differentiate between question purposes within specific cases.

LLM-Based Semantic Clustering. To address these limitations, we employed an LLM-based approach inspired by Didolkar et al. [17]. First, we filtered out "incoherent" questions - i.e. those requiring additional context beyond the opening statement to be meaningful. Then, we prompted Llama 3.1-70B to label each question with a descriptive "purpose" in the context of the opening statement. Similar to Didolkar et al. [17], we found that this approach resulted in too many fine-grained labels (∼4000). Subsequently, we prompted Llama 3.1-70B to perform semantic clustering, grouping similar purpose labels into broader, coarse-grained categories with brief descriptions. This reduced the set to ∼250 intermediate labels. A second round of semantic clustering further consolidated these into a final set of 7 purpose categories. Table 4 lists the final seven categories and their descriptions derived through this process. This process is visualized in Figure 14. Since this automated purpose discovery and semantic clustering methodology was inspired by Didolkar et al. [17], we refer to this question type diversity metric as Metacog in our study. Figure 17 shows the distribution of generated turns for all simulators across the Metacog categories.

B.4.3 Stetson Classification. The Stetson University College of Law published a 2018 Oral Argument advocacy guide [5]. Chapter 5 details the most common types of oral argument questions. We use these categories to define the Stetson classification scheme used for evaluating question type diversity. We summarize these question categories in Table 5. ## B.5 Fallacy Detection

We expect justices to push back against advocates whose statements contain common logical fallacies. To test this, we construct a semisynthetic benchmark with GPT4o.

Dataset Construction. We take an opening statement and generate a justice question to it, sampling one of the nine justices at random for each generation. Then, we go through a list of common logical fallacies found on the LSAT and generate an advocate response, with each response incorporating a logical fallacy. All synthetically generated samples were manually reviewed for quality. The test set consists of samples across 10 different fallacy types:

(1) factual–general: The argument relies on a factual claim that is inaccurate or directly contradicted by the known facts. (2) factual–legal: The argument misstates, misapplies, or inaccurately cites a legal rule, precedent, or holding. (3) correlation-vs-causation: The argument assumes that because two events occur together or in sequence, one caused the other. (4) sufficient-vs-necessary: The argument confuses necessary conditions with sufficient conditions, treating one as if it were the other. (5) comparison: The argument treats two things as equivalent based on superficial similarities while ignoring relevant differences (false analogy). (6) sampling: The argument draws a general conclusion from an unrepresentative, biased, or insufficient sample. (7) exclusivity: The argument presents only two options as if they are exhaustive, ignoring additional plausible alternatives (false dichotomy). (8) numbers: The argument improperly compares quantities by conflating absolute numbers with percentages or proportions. (9) ignoring-justice: The response fails to address the substance of the question posed, instead shifting to an irrelevant or tangential point. (10) misstating-justice: The response reframes or alters the question being asked and then answers that different question, rather than addressing the question as posed.

Experimental Setup. Like in the adversarial testing for realism setting, we evaluate simulators on this test set by generating a justice response to the purposefully set advocate turn. We construct a human-reviewed explanation of the exact error made by the advocate in each of the logical fallacy samples. Finally, we use Qwen3-32B as the judge model to classify whether the generated justice response successfully caught the error made in the advocate’s last turn.

## B.6 Tone of Questioning

We use the Valence metric to assess tone of questioning. Specifically, we prompt Qwen3-32B to classify each question as one of {Competitive, Slightly Competitive, Neutral, Slightly Supportive and Supportive}. We then bucket the first two and the last two labels to get three possible labels for each response: {Competitive, Neutral, Supportive}. This classification provides insight into whether a specific justice is likely to respond negatively or favorably to a lawyer’s position. Such information is particularly valuable for lawyers preparing oral arguments, as it helps anticipate and strategize for potential judicial reactions ([36, 52]).
